abstract: One of the benefits of shared decision-making is that it can resolve conflicting preferences among group members. This allows the members of moving animal groups to maintain cohesion while deciding on where to go next. However, followers are faced with decisions that vary in complexity. At some times followers only have a single initiator to choose from, while at other times they may have to select among multiple simultaneous initiators each moving in different directions. One question is whether increased disagreement, in terms of the number and spread of directions among initiators, has an impact on the time it takes for followers to make their move. Here I use whole-group GPS tracking datasets from vulturine guineafowl (Acryllium vulturinum) and olive baboons (Papio anubis) to link the complexity of the decision arising from disagreement to the time it takes for followers to resolve a movement decision. Across both species, there is a significant impact of having more initiating directions, with every additional direction adding approximately 11 s (for 1 direction) to 99 s (for 9 directions) on decision time. This suggests that both suffer from the paradox of choice. In vulturine guineafowl, high directional conflict also added up to 162 s on decision times relative to low direction conflict, whereas baboons appeared unaffected by directional conflict. Overall, these results confirm that within-group disagreement among initiators can increase the complexity of decisions faced by followers, and that this ultimately increases the time needed to resolve movement decisions.
